profile.address: West Military Drive, San Antonio, Bexar County, Texas, 78245
profile.reading:
NSA Texas, formally the Texas Cryptologic Center, is one of the National Security Agency's cryptologic centers in the United States, alongside the agency's Fort Meade, Maryland headquarters and the Utah Data Center at Camp Williams. The San Antonio facility sits on the Medina Annex of what is now Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland and occupies a building with an unusual origin, a semiconductor fabrication plant Sony built and then closed in 2003. The NSA selected the shuttered Sony plant for its own use in 2005, a point at which the project was still discussed relatively openly in local reporting, and filed its first building permits with the city in May 2006 before the program's profile receded from public view.

Reporting based on a 2006 municipal bond document put the projected investment in converting and expanding the site at up to 300 million dollars. The building grew substantially during that buildout, from roughly 498,000 square feet across two connected structures to approximately 633,000 square feet, an expansion that included a dedicated 94,000 square foot data storage complex completed in June 2010. The facility became fully operational in late 2012. Bexar County property records tracked the site's assessed value rising from about 33.5 million dollars in 2008 to more than 72 million dollars as the buildout progressed, and the lease rate reported for the property, 34.69 dollars per square foot, ran well above San Antonio's citywide average of roughly 21.52 dollars at the time.

The project was projected to bring around 1,500 new jobs to San Antonio, on top of an estimated 2,000 military personnel and civilians the NSA relocated to the area from Lackland facilities as the program stood up in 2005. Consistent with the agency's practice for its cryptologic centers, the facility's funding does not appear as a line item in the Department of Defense's unclassified budget, and independent reviews of federal budget documents from 2004 through 2013 were unable to identify its funding source. As a signals intelligence and cyberwarfare facility, the Texas Cryptologic Center publishes no capacity, tenancy, or commercial specifications of the kind a colocation data center would, because it is not a commercial facility, and its technical specifications are classified rather than simply undisclosed. The clearest public record of the site therefore consists of property and permitting records, contemporaneous local press coverage of its construction, and a single, unrelated 2010 news item in which nearby residents reported that an NSA antenna was interfering with their garage door openers, a small but concrete data point confirming active signals equipment on site at that time.

reading.body:
The Texas Cryptologic Center is a signals intelligence and cyberwarfare facility operated by the National Security Agency on the grounds of Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, not a commercial data center, and publishes no capacity specifications. The site occupies a converted Sony semiconductor fabrication plant that was shuttered in 2003. The NSA acquired it in 2005, filed building permits in May 2006, and brought the facility to full operational status in late 2012 after an expansion that grew the structure from roughly 498,000 square feet to approximately 633,000 square feet, including a dedicated 94,000 square foot data storage complex completed in June 2010.

The agency's investment in converting and expanding the site was projected at up to 300 million dollars based on a 2006 municipal bond document. The assessed property value rose from approximately 33.5 million dollars in 2008 to more than 72 million dollars as construction proceeded. A 2010 news report that nearby residents' garage door openers were interfered with by an NSA antenna provides concrete confirmation that active signals equipment was on site at that time. The facility's technical specifications are classified, and its funding does not appear as a line item in the Department of Defense's unclassified budget, so its power consumption and computational capacity cannot be determined from public records.

Because this facility publishes no power or capacity figures, it does not appear in the 18 Texas data center campuses with published megawatt specifications and therefore cannot be ranked by power consumption among the state's commercial colocation landscape. The state context provided does not include defense or classified government facilities in its mapping. For readers assessing AI scaling constraints, this site is not relevant to the analysis, because the binding constraint on AI is grid capacity available to the commercial compute sector, and the NSA's classified infrastructure operates under different procurement, power, and planning rules than commercial data center operations.
